text.p: Copper prices charged to 2-1/2 month highs during a busy LME session on Friday.

Gold recovered slightly from a sell-off in London after strong gains earlier in the week and oil prices consolidated recent gains as traders took stock of its giddy climb and amid signs of a respite in the colder weather of winter in the U.S.
But wheat prices closed lower with a thin market hit by late selling despite optimistic export news.
The CRB index closed 1.29 points higher at 244.70.

Copper prices charged higher during an extremely active Friday LME session with prices hitting the highest for 2-1/2 months on waves of fund buying, shortcovering and option delta purchases. The market rose in excess of five percent, ranging from $2,010 to $2,152 before closing at $2,148 a tonne, a gain of $117 from Thursday. Declining warehouse inventories and widening backwardations induced the dramatic moves. "Copper was the only game in town today - the others hardly moved in comparison. Everybody is a bit shell-shocked now," one trader said. Traders said the market has largely discounted reports earlier this week of a large hidden stockpile and is focussing on dwindling visible stocks. LME inventories fell by 8,000 tonnes to a new 6-1/4 year low of 101,175 tonnes. Confirmation of a decline kicked the market higher, with the lack of a sizeable tonnage delivered into Singapore also supportive.

Elsewhere, the other metals took a back seat, with aluminium clawing its way towards $1,450 after a stock decline. Last trade was at $1,442, up $14. Nickel prices fell throughout the session, initially responding to a 570-tonne stock increase, then on chart selling. The market is now vulnerable to a challenge of the $7,000 level on the downside. Last kerb trade was at $7,050 a tonne, down $110 from Thursday.

The zinc market made gradual upward progress today, with momentum from copper enough to see prices residing above $1,060 by the end of the session. News Spain's Asturiana had finally liquidated its LME futures position came as no surprise as this operation had been continuing for some time. But with this large market position, which dates back to the early 1990s out of the way, there is more scope for longer-term upside movement. Last trade was at $1,064, up $4.50. Lead's attempts to push higher faltered above $730, and by the end of the kerb the market was back at an unchanged $725. Tin was supported by an inventory decline of 260 tonnes, with speculative buying lifting prices above $6,000. Last trade was at $6,060, up $80.

New York precious metals futures ended off the day's lows Friday as silver recovered late in the session, after the complex opened lower for the second day in a row. "There has been some more producer selling in gold today, as well as some fund selling," Credit Suisse New York vice president Ian MacDonald said. "Your're likely to see more producer selling on the way back up, and the funds don't have much reason to reverse their record short positions yet," he said. "But on other hand gold doesn't seem to want to go much below $378-380, so we may be going to trade a range for a while," he said. COMEX December gold closed down 70 cents at $381.10, after recovering partially from intraday lows at $379.80. Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $380.05/380.55, compared to the London afternoon fix Friday at $379.25 and the New York close Thursday around $381.00/381.40. Gold sold off Thursday, bringing to an end a six day recovery from 18 month lows at $376.80 seen in late October.

World oil prices paused for breath on Friday as traders took stock of its giddy climb and amid signs of some respite in the deepening gloom of winter in the U.S. World benchmark Brent crude futures for January were valued at $23.45 per barrel, 15 cents down on the day and still well over $1 below October's six-year high of $25.06. "I think this is more of a pause than anything else," said Tim Holmes of MeesPierson derivatives. Fresh news of larger than expected supplies of North Sea oil in December also helped take a little of the shine off what has otherwise been a ferocious autumn rally. December crude stood 23 cents a barrels lower at $24.18.

CBOT wheat futures closed mostly lower on a sharp drop in the KCBT and MGE markets. "Kansas City December and Minneapolis got blasted, so that hurt us here," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. KCBT December ended six cents lower and MGE December dropped 4-1/4 cents. Traders said the volume was thin throughout the day which left the market vulnerable for the late slide that mainly was triggered by local selling.
The late break occurred despite optimistic export news.

"We talk about no wheat business yet we continue to see nearly one-half million tonnes every week and I think it's very constructive," said Mark Cermak, of O'Connor and Co. USDA Friday said the net export sales for wheat during the week ended November 7 totaled 474.9 million tonnes, above trade expectations for 300,000 to 350,000 tonnes. Wheat also was underpinned by hints of a brighter export outlook with the European Union this week cutting back on the amount of subsidy for wheat exports. Wheat closed 2-1/4 cents per bushel lower to 1/2 higher, with December up 1/2 at $3.97-1/4.
